source.title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering

claims.summary: Open-domain QA can use a two-stage retriever-reader pipeline: retrieve a small candidate set, then inspect it for the answer.
Sparse term matching is effective for exact keywords, while dense representations can connect semantically related text without exact token overlap.
The paper asks whether a strong dense embedding model can be trained from question-passage or question-answer supervision without additional pretraining.
The authors claim that the selected training setup lets a simple dense retriever outperform BM25 and that improved retrieval can improve end-to-end QA.
DPR uses separate question and passage encoders and ranks passages using the inner product of their vectors.
Passage embeddings are computed and indexed offline; at runtime the question embedding is used to retrieve nearby passages with FAISS.
In-batch negatives reuse other questions' positive passages as negatives, and the best reported training setup also includes a BM25 hard negative.
The retrieval unit is a passage rather than a whole document; the experiment uses fixed-length, non-overlapping text blocks with article titles prepended.
Top-k retrieval accuracy is the fraction of questions for which at least one of the top-k retrieved passages contains an answer span.
On the Natural Questions test set in the Single setting, Top-20 retrieval accuracy is 78.4 for DPR and 59.1 for BM25.

claims.summary: The qualitative analysis says dense retrieval captures lexical variation and semantic relations better, but can miss rare salient phrases that term matching captures.
The paper studies retrieval for open-domain extractive QA, where the final answer is a span in a retrieved passage; it is not itself a complete generative RAG model.
